intro: In the last unit, prices moved freely. When lemonade got popular, its price rose; when concert tickets were scarce, resale prices jumped. This unit asks what happens when a price is not allowed to move, and what happens when a price moves freely but still leaves something out. A gas station in 1973 with a line around the block, an apartment with forty applicants, a river that turned brown below a paper mill, and a fireworks show nobody would pay for are all part of the same story.

The first chapter looks at price ceilings and price floors: rent control, the minimum wage, farm price supports and the gasoline lines of the 1970s. You will see why a ceiling below the market price creates a shortage, why a floor above it creates a surplus, and what takes the place of price when price cannot ration: lines, lotteries, favoritism and black markets. You will also see who really pays a tax. The second chapter looks at market failure: pollution and other externalities, public goods and free riders, overused common resources, and deals where one side knows more than the other.

By the end, you will be able to take a real policy, such as a cap on rents, a tax on pollution or a subsidy for flu shots, and predict what it does with numbers. You will be able to say who gains, who loses and what the policy costs. Economists do not all agree on these questions, and neither will your classmates. The goal is not one right opinion. The goal is to argue from the model and the numbers, and to name the trade-offs honestly.
bigQuestion: When should government step into a market, by setting prices, taxing, regulating or providing goods itself, and how can we tell if it made things better or worse?

timeline.t: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations names public works that no private person would build as a duty of government
Arthur Pigou's The Economics of Welfare argues for taxing costs that spill onto others
The Agricultural Adjustment Act begins federal programs to hold up farm prices
The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the first federal minimum wage, 25 cents an hour
Wartime ration books and price controls cover sugar, meat, gasoline and tires
Paul Samuelson gives the modern definition of a public good
Ronald Coase shows how clear property rights and bargaining can settle some spillover costs
Garrett Hardin names the tragedy of the commons
The EPA is created, and George Akerlof publishes his paper on lemons and hidden quality
An oil embargo and price controls on gasoline bring long lines at the pump
Federal price controls on oil and gasoline end, and the lines do not return
The Clean Air Act Amendments create a cap-and-trade market to cut sulfur dioxide

words.d: a legal maximum price; it creates a shortage only when it is set below the equilibrium price
a legal minimum price; it creates a surplus only when it is set above the equilibrium price
a price control is binding when it actually changes the market price: a ceiling below equilibrium or a floor above it
the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a price held below equilibrium
the amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a price held above equilibrium
buying and selling at prices or in ways the law forbids, which grows wherever a price control binds
who actually bears a tax after prices adjust; the less elastic side of the market bears more
a cost or benefit of a deal that falls on people who were not part of it, such as pollution or the protection from a vaccine
the full cost of producing something: the producer's private cost plus the external cost to others
a good that is non-rival and non-excludable, such as national defense, which markets tend not to provide
someone who enjoys a good without paying for it because nobody can keep them from using it
the overuse of a resource that everyone may use and nobody owns, because each user ignores the cost to others

test.q: A city caps downtown parking at $2 an hour where the market rate would be $5. What is the most likely result?
choices: No change, because the cap is non-binding
Drivers circle for a long time looking for spaces that are almost always full
test.why: A ceiling below equilibrium binds and creates a shortage. Time spent circling takes over the rationing job the price cannot do.

test.q: At a $6 price floor, sellers offer 500 units and buyers want 350. What does the floor create?
test.why: Surplus = quantity supplied minus quantity demanded = 500 - 350 = 150 units.

test.q: When the price of lumber rises, sawmills add a second shift because they can now earn more. Which job of a price is this?
test.why: A higher price rewards producers for making more. That is the motivate job.

test.q: A 50-cent tax per pack of batteries is collected from sellers. The price buyers pay rises from $5.00 to $5.10. Who bears more of the tax?
test.why: Buyers pay $0.10 more. Sellers keep $5.10 - $0.50 = $4.60, which is $0.40 less than before, so sellers bear more.

test.q: Which statement best describes what economists say about the minimum wage?
choices: All agree a moderate increase destroys many jobs
All agree it has no effect on jobs
The simple model predicts fewer jobs, and economists disagree about how large the effect is for moderate increases
All agree it lowers the pay of workers who keep their jobs
test.why: The price-floor model predicts a surplus of labor. Studies of moderate increases give mixed results, so the size of the effect is debated.

test.q: Over ten years, what usually happens to the housing shortage under a binding rent control?
choices: It disappears as renters leave the city
It grows, because fewer rental units are built and existing ones are kept up less
It stays the same, because housing supply never changes
test.why: Housing supply is inelastic in the short run but responds over time. A capped rent discourages building and upkeep, so supply shrinks.

test.q: A concert venue's private cost is $20 per ticket sold, and the noise imposes $5 of harm per ticket on neighbors. What is the social cost per ticket?
test.why: Social cost = private cost + external cost = $20 + $5 = $25.

test.q: Which of these is closest to a pure public good?
choices: A flood-control levee that protects a whole town
test.why: A levee protects everyone behind it at once (non-rival), and no one in town can be left unprotected (non-excludable).

test.q: Why do many governments subsidize flu shots?
choices: Flu shots have a negative externality
Flu shots cannot be sold in a market
Buyers leave out the protection their shot gives to others, so the market provides too few
test.why: A positive externality means social benefit is above private benefit. A subsidy lowers the price so more people get the shot.

test.q: In a cap-and-trade system, what does the government fix?
choices: The total amount of pollution allowed
The cleanup cost at each plant
The number of firms in the industry
test.why: The cap sets the total number of permits, so total pollution is fixed. The permit price is left to the market.

test.q: Why do open-access fisheries tend to be overfished?
choices: Each fisher ignores how his catch reduces what is left for everyone else
Fish prices are held down by law
test.why: In a commons, each user bears only his own costs, not the cost his use imposes on others. That leads to overuse.

test.q: An insurer prices a plan for the average person. Mostly people who expect big medical bills sign up, and healthy people skip it. What is this called?
test.why: When buyers know more about their own risk than the seller does, the people who show up to buy are the most costly ones.

test.q: A city caps concert tickets at $40, and on show night tickets resell outside for $150. What caused the resale market?
choices: A price floor that created a surplus
A binding price ceiling that created a shortage
A fall in demand for the concert
test.why: The cap held the price below equilibrium. Fans who could not buy at $40 bid up the tickets that leaked out.

test.q: A small group of producers spends millions lobbying to keep a program that raises their prices and costs each consumer a few dollars a year. What is this called?
test.why: Rent-seeking is spending effort to win favors from government instead of producing. Concentrated gains organize; scattered losses do not.

test.q: Under a price ceiling on gasoline, a driver waits 3 hours to save $6. What did her waiting earn per hour?
test.why: $6 saved ÷ 3 hours = $2 an hour. Rationing by waiting costs time that no seller receives.

write.prompt: Your city council proposes capping one-bedroom rents at $1,200 a month where the market rent is $1,600. Make up a small supply-and-demand table, predict the shortage now and in ten years, compare rent control with one other tool such as a housing voucher or allowing more building, and argue which you would choose.
tips: Say whether the cap is binding and show the shortage with numbers from your table.
Explain why supply changes little in year one but more over ten years.
Name who gains and who loses: tenants with leases, newcomers, landlords, taxpayers.
Describe how apartments get rationed if price cannot do it: waiting lists, key fees, favoritism.
Give the strongest argument for the side you did not choose, then say why yours wins.

title: Prices, Controls and Market Failure

chapters.title: Ceilings, Floors and Rationing
chapters.bigQuestion: When a government says a price may not rise or may not fall, what happens to the people the rule was meant to help?

story.title: The Winter the Pumps Ran Dry
story.kicker: In the 1970s, American drivers waited in lines that stretched around the block, and the reason was not only a lack of oil.
paragraphs: Picture a Tuesday morning in the winter of 1973. A driver in a Chicago suburb pulls into a gas station at 6:30 a.m. and finds forty cars already ahead of her. The engine idles. The line creeps forward one car length at a time. After an hour and a half she reaches the pump, and the attendant tells her the limit is ten gallons. At the station across the street, a hand-painted sign says only two words: NO GAS.

The trouble began that October. Several oil-producing countries in the Middle East stopped shipping oil to the United States after a war in the region. World oil prices jumped. Less oil came in, so less gasoline could be refined. Everyone expected gasoline to get expensive. That part was simple scarcity: there was less of the stuff to go around.

But the United States also had rules left over from a program of wage and price controls that had started in 1971. Those rules put a legal lid on what stations could charge for gasoline. The price was not allowed to climb to the level where buyers and sellers would match up. At the controlled price, drivers wanted far more gasoline than stations could get. The gap showed up as a line of cars.

States tried other ways to decide who got fuel. Many adopted odd-even rules: a car with a license plate ending in an odd number could buy on odd-numbered days, an even plate on even days. Some stations closed on Sundays. Some sold only to regular customers. Drivers topped off half-full tanks out of fear, which made the lines longer still. The same scene came back in 1979 after a revolution in Iran cut world supply again.

In the early 1980s the federal government removed the price controls on oil and gasoline. Prices rose, and then something happened that surprised many people. The lines vanished. Oil was still scarce, as it always is, but there was no longer a shortage at the pump. The difference between those two words, scarce and shortage, is the heart of this chapter.
story.think: Gasoline was scarce both before and after the controls ended. Why did the lines exist only while the price was held down?

lessons.title: Three Jobs of a Price
lessons.mainIdea: A market price does three jobs at once: it signals, it rations and it motivates.
reading: In June, strawberries at a farm stand near Kankakee sell for about $3 a pound. Suppose a late frost wipes out half the local crop. Within a week the price at the stand is $6 a pound. Nobody held a meeting to set that number. The higher price appeared because many buyers were chasing far fewer berries. That price is now doing three jobs at the same time.

First, the price is a *signal*. A $6 tag tells every grower in the country that strawberries are in short supply in Illinois. A farm in a warmer state that was going to sell its berries locally now ships a truckload north instead. Second, the price *rations*. At $3 the stand sold about 1,000 pounds a day. At $6 the buyers who wanted berries for a single snack drop out, and daily sales fall to about 600 pounds. The limited berries go to the people who value them most, as measured by what they will pay.

Third, the price *motivates*. The chance to earn $6 a pound pushes growers to replant damaged rows, water more carefully and pick fields that were not worth picking at $3. Over the summer, extra supply arrives and the price drifts back down. No one was ordered to do any of this. The price carried the information and the reward in one number. When a government freezes a price, all three jobs stop working, and this chapter is about what happens next.

words.d: information a price sends to buyers and sellers about how scarce a good has become
to decide who gets a limited good; a price rations by letting those willing to pay have it
to give a reason to act; a higher price motivates sellers to produce more

look.title: A Price Jumps Overnight
look.text: A hurricane knocks out power in a coastal city. Before the storm, a bag of ice sold for $2. The morning after, the only open store is charging $8 a bag. Some shoppers call this unfair. A truck driver 300 miles away hears about the $8 price and loads his refrigerated trailer with ice.
look.prompt: Name the three jobs the $8 price is doing in this scene. Then say what might happen if the city ordered the store to charge $2.

check.q: After the frost, strawberry sales at the stand fell from 1,000 pounds a day to 600. Which job of a price does this show?
choices: Rationing: the higher price decided who got the limited berries
Signaling to growers in other states
Lowering the cost of growing berries
check.why: When the price rose, some buyers dropped out and the scarce berries went to those willing to pay $6. That is rationing by price.

check.q: A farm in a warmer state ships berries north after hearing about the $6 price. Which job of a price is at work?
choices: Signaling that berries are scarce in Illinois
check.why: The high price carried information to distant growers that berries were scarce in Illinois. That is the signal job.

check.q: Why did the strawberry price drift back toward $3 over the summer?
choices: The government set a new price
The high price motivated more supply, and more berries pushed the price down
The frost destroyed the remaining crop
check.why: The $6 price motivated growers to replant and ship more. Extra supply then lowered the price. That is the motivate job followed by the market adjusting.

lessons.title: A Market That Clears
lessons.mainIdea: Left alone, a price moves toward the level where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is no shortage and no surplus.
reading: Think about used bikes in a college town in August. Here is a labeled example schedule. At $100, students want 90 bikes but only 30 owners will sell. At $150, buyers want 70 and sellers offer 50. At $200, buyers want 60 and sellers offer 60. At $250, buyers want 50 and sellers offer 70. The price where the two numbers match, $200 and 60 bikes, is the *equilibrium*. Economists say the market *clears* at that price: every buyer who wants a bike at $200 finds a seller, and every seller who wants to sell at $200 finds a buyer.

Now suppose sellers try $250. They offer 70 bikes but buyers take only 50. The extra 20 bikes are a *surplus*. Sellers with unsold bikes cut their asking price to attract a buyer, and the price falls toward $200. Suppose instead the price starts at $150. Buyers want 70 bikes but only 50 are offered. The missing 20 bikes are a *shortage*. Buyers who cannot find a bike offer a little more, sellers notice, and the price rises toward $200.

Notice what a shortage is and is not. It is not the same as scarcity. Bikes are always scarce; there are never enough for everyone to have one free. A shortage is a gap between what buyers want and what sellers offer at one particular price. A free-moving price closes that gap by itself. A shortage lasts only when something stops the price from rising. In the rest of this chapter, that something is usually a law.

words.d: the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so the market has no reason to move
a market clears when every willing buyer and seller at the going price finds a match
the amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a price above equilibrium
the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a price below equilibrium

look.title: Used Bikes in August (labeled example)
look.cite: An invented schedule for a college-town used-bike market, built for this lesson.
look.prompt: At $150, how big is the shortage? At $250, how big is the surplus? Which way does the price move in each case, and why?

check.q: In the bike schedule, what is the equilibrium price and quantity?
check.why: At $200 quantity demanded (60) equals quantity supplied (60). At every other price the two numbers differ.

check.q: At a price of $150, how many bikes short is the market?
check.why: Shortage = quantity demanded minus quantity supplied = 70 - 50 = 20 bikes.

check.q: Which statement about scarcity and shortage is correct?
choices: Scarcity is always true; a shortage exists only at a price below equilibrium
A shortage exists at every price; scarcity only in a crisis
Scarcity disappears when the market clears
check.why: Scarcity is permanent: wants exceed resources. A shortage is a gap at one specific price and disappears when the price is free to rise.

lessons.title: A Ceiling That Binds
lessons.mainIdea: A price ceiling set below equilibrium creates a shortage; a ceiling set above equilibrium does nothing.
reading: A *price ceiling* is a legal maximum price. Sellers may charge less but not more. Go back to the used-bike schedule from the last lesson, where the market clears at $200. Suppose the city council decides bikes are too expensive for students and passes a rule: no used bike may sell for more than $150. At $150, buyers want 70 bikes and sellers offer 50. The rule has manufactured a shortage of 20 bikes that did not exist before.

The word to remember is *binding*. A ceiling binds only when it sits below the equilibrium price. Suppose the council had set the ceiling at $250 instead. The market clears at $200, which is already under the cap, so nothing changes. Students sometimes picture a ceiling as something above the market, because a ceiling in a room is above your head. In economics the effective ceiling is below equilibrium, holding the price down like a lid. A ceiling above equilibrium is called non-binding.

What happens to the 20 students who want a bike at $150 but cannot get one? The price is no longer allowed to ration, so something else will. Some students will camp out at the bike shop early. Some sellers will keep bikes for friends. Some will quietly sell for $220 in a parking lot. Sellers who must accept $150 may stop fixing brakes or replacing tires before a sale, because the lower price does not pay for the work. Every one of these results shows up wherever a ceiling binds, from apartments to gasoline.

words.d: a legal maximum price; sellers may charge less but not more
a price control is binding when it actually changes the market price; a ceiling binds only below equilibrium
a price control that sits on the wrong side of equilibrium and therefore has no effect

look.title: Two Ceilings, One Market
look.text: Bottled water in a small town clears at $1.50 a bottle. After a flood scare, the town passes a law: no store may charge more than $2.00 a bottle. Two weeks later, demand surges and the market price would have risen to $3.00 if it were free. The $2.00 law is still in force.
look.prompt: Was the ceiling binding when it passed? Is it binding two weeks later? Describe what the shelves probably look like in each case.

check.q: In the bike market that clears at $200, a legal maximum of $150 is set. What results?
choices: No change, because the ceiling is non-binding
check.why: At $150, quantity demanded is 70 and quantity supplied is 50. The shortage is 70 - 50 = 20 bikes.

check.q: A city sets a price ceiling of $250 on used bikes when the equilibrium is $200. What happens?
choices: Nothing; the ceiling is non-binding because it is above equilibrium
check.why: A ceiling only binds when it is below the equilibrium price. The market already clears at $200, under the cap.

check.q: Under a binding ceiling, why might sellers stop fixing brakes before selling a bike?
choices: The lower legal price no longer pays for the extra work, so quality falls
check.why: When the price is capped, sellers cannot be paid for extra quality, so they cut it. Falling quality is a standard hidden cost of a binding ceiling.

lessons.title: Rent Control
lessons.mainIdea: Rent control is a price ceiling on apartments: it helps tenants who already have a lease and tends to shrink the supply of housing over time.
reading: Imagine a city where the market rent for a one-bedroom apartment is $1,500 a month and 10,000 such apartments are rented. Rents have been climbing, and voters pass *rent control*: no landlord may charge more than $1,000. Here is a labeled example of what happens. At $1,000, renters want 12,000 apartments. Landlords, however, will offer only 9,000; some convert units to condos, some stop renting a basement unit, some sell. The shortage is 12,000 - 9,000 = 3,000 apartments.

The shortage grows with time. In the first year, most buildings already exist, so supply barely changes. Economists say short-run supply is *inelastic*. But over ten years, builders decide not to put up new rental buildings when the rent cannot cover the cost. Owners skimp on paint, heat and repairs, because a full waiting list means a leaky faucet will not cost them a tenant. The 3,000-unit shortage may double. Meanwhile newcomers, young workers and people who move for a job cannot find a place at all, while a lucky tenant in a controlled unit stays put for decades.

This is a case where the arguments deserve a fair hearing on both sides. Supporters say rent control protects long-time residents from sudden rent spikes, keeps neighborhoods stable and prevents families from being pushed out of the city they grew up in. They point out that building takes years and tenants need help now. Critics answer that the control helps only those who already hold a lease, shrinks the supply of housing and lowers its quality, and that the real fix is to allow more building. Most economists lean toward the critics on the supply question, but many also support other tenant protections such as help with moving costs or rent vouchers, which do not cap the price.

words.d: a law setting a maximum rent a landlord may charge; a price ceiling on housing
not very responsive to price; short-run housing supply is inelastic because buildings take years to add or remove
government money given to a household to help pay for something, such as rent, without capping the price

look.title: Two Neighbors
look.text: Maria has lived in a rent-controlled apartment for 22 years and pays $900 for a place that would rent for $2,100 on the open market. Her nephew Luis just took a job downtown and has spent three months looking. Every affordable listing has forty applicants, and one landlord hinted he would sign with whoever paid a $3,000 cash 'key fee.'
look.prompt: Who is the control helping, who is it hurting, and what is the key fee an example of? What would a rent voucher change for Luis?

check.q: In the example, rent control at $1,000 leads to 12,000 apartments demanded and 9,000 supplied. What is the shortage?
check.why: Shortage = quantity demanded minus quantity supplied = 12,000 - 9,000 = 3,000.

check.q: Why does the housing shortage under rent control tend to grow over ten years?
choices: The government raises the ceiling every year
Builders stop adding rental units and owners let buildings decline, so supply shrinks
check.why: Supply is inelastic in the short run but responds over time. When rent cannot cover costs, fewer units get built or kept up.

check.q: Which policy helps a renter pay without setting a legal maximum rent?
check.why: A voucher gives the household money to pay rent. It raises what the renter can afford but leaves the market price free to move.

lessons.title: Gas Lines, Explained
lessons.mainIdea: The 1970s gasoline lines were a shortage created by a binding price ceiling on top of real scarcity.
reading: The chapter opened with drivers waiting ninety minutes for ten gallons. Here is the same story in the language you now have. In 1973 world oil supply fell, so the supply curve for gasoline shifted left. In a free market the price would have jumped to a new, higher equilibrium. Fewer people would have driven, more would have carpooled, and the smaller amount of gasoline would have been rationed by price. There would have been complaints about the price, but no lines.

Instead, federal rules held the price at the pump below that new equilibrium. Suppose, as a labeled example, the controlled price was $0.40 a gallon while the market-clearing price would have been $0.60. At $0.40, drivers wanted more gasoline than refiners could deliver. That gap was the *shortage*, and it took the form of lines, limits per customer and stations with no gas at all. The price could not do its rationing job, so time did it instead. Waiting in line was a cost, but one that went to nobody. Nobody got paid for the hours that drivers sat idling.

When the controls were lifted in the early 1980s, the price rose to where the market cleared, and the lines disappeared even though oil was no more plentiful. The lesson is not that high prices are pleasant. It is that a *price control* does not create more of a scarce good. It only changes how the scarce good gets divided, from willingness to pay to willingness to wait. Any policy that wants to help drivers has to either increase supply or accept some other way of choosing who gets the gasoline.

words.d: the gap between what buyers want and what sellers offer at a price held below equilibrium
any law that fixes a maximum or minimum price instead of letting the market set it
a sudden event that shifts the supply curve, such as an oil embargo or a crop failure

look.title: The Odd-Even Rule
look.text: During the 1970s shortages, many states let cars with odd-numbered license plates buy gas only on odd-numbered days, and even plates on even days. Lines got somewhat shorter. Some drivers bought a second car with a plate ending in the other kind of number. Others filled gas cans on their allowed day.
look.prompt: Did the odd-even rule change the amount of gasoline available? What did it change? Why did some drivers respond by buying a second car?

check.q: In 1973 the supply of oil fell. In a market with no price controls, what would have happened at the pump?
choices: The price would have risen to a new equilibrium and there would have been no lines
The price would have fallen and lines would have formed
A surplus of gasoline would have appeared
check.why: A leftward supply shift raises the equilibrium price. A free price rations the smaller supply without a shortage, so no lines.

check.q: With the price held at $0.40 while the market would clear at $0.60, what rationed gasoline instead of price?
choices: Willingness to wait in line and limits per customer
check.why: When a ceiling binds, price cannot ration. Time in line, per-customer limits and luck took over the job.

check.q: When gasoline price controls ended in the early 1980s, why did the lines vanish even though oil was still scarce?
choices: The price rose to the level where quantity demanded equaled quantity supplied
check.why: A free price rises until the market clears. Scarcity remained, but the shortage, which is a gap at a fixed price, disappeared.

lessons.title: A Floor That Binds
lessons.mainIdea: A price floor set above equilibrium creates a surplus; a floor set below equilibrium does nothing.
reading: A *price floor* is a legal minimum price. Sellers may charge more but not less. Here is a labeled example for a dairy market. Milk clears at $3 a gallon, where 1,000 gallons a day are bought and sold in a small city. Farmers complain that $3 does not cover their costs, and the state sets a floor of $4. At $4, farmers supply 1,200 gallons, because the higher price makes it worth milking more cows. Shoppers, facing $4, buy only 900 gallons. The result is a *surplus* of 1,200 - 900 = 300 gallons a day.

Just like a ceiling, a floor only matters when it is on the binding side of equilibrium. A floor at $4 binds because it is above the $3 clearing price. A floor at $2 would be non-binding: the market already trades at $3, so a rule saying the price may not fall below $2 changes nothing. Students often mix this up, so say it twice. Ceilings bind from below. Floors bind from above.

Who deals with the 300 extra gallons? In a free market the price would fall until the milk cleared, but the floor forbids that. So either the milk spoils, the government buys it, or farmers find some other way to compete for the buyers who remain. They might offer free delivery or coupons, which quietly lower the real price. Every binding floor produces a surplus, and every surplus needs an answer. The next two lessons look at the two most famous floors in the American economy: the minimum wage and farm price supports.

words.d: a legal minimum price; sellers may charge more but not less
the amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a price above equilibrium
the amount sellers offer for sale at one specific price

look.title: Milk With and Without a Floor (labeled example)
look.cite: An invented schedule for a small-city milk market, built for this lesson.
look.prompt: How large is the surplus at a $4 floor? At a $5 floor? What happens with a floor at $2, and why?

check.q: Milk clears at $3. The state sets a floor of $4, where 1,200 gallons are supplied and 900 demanded. What results?
choices: No change; the floor is non-binding
check.why: Surplus = quantity supplied minus quantity demanded = 1,200 - 900 = 300 gallons a day.

check.q: A price floor of $2 is set in a milk market that clears at $3. What happens?
choices: Nothing; a floor below equilibrium is non-binding
check.why: Floors bind only from above. The market trades at $3, so a rule against prices below $2 has no effect.

check.q: Under a binding floor, why might dairies start offering free delivery or coupons?
choices: It is a way to compete for buyers by quietly lowering the real price
check.why: Sellers cannot legally cut the posted price, so they compete with extras that lower the effective price. This is a common response to a surplus.

lessons.title: The Minimum Wage Debate
lessons.mainIdea: The minimum wage is a price floor on labor; the simple model predicts fewer jobs, and economists disagree about how large that effect is in practice.
reading: A wage is the price of an hour of work. In the *labor market*, workers are the sellers and employers are the buyers, so the picture flips from a normal market: households supply labor and businesses demand it. The federal *minimum wage* has been $7.25 an hour since 2009. Illinois raised its own minimum in steps, reaching $15 an hour in 2025. A minimum wage is a price floor, and the tools from the last lesson apply.

Here is a labeled example for one town. Suppose the market wage for entry-level restaurant work would clear at $12 an hour with 1,000 jobs. The state sets a floor of $15. At $15, employers want only 900 workers; a few restaurants cut hours, install ordering kiosks or close a slow lunch shift. At $15, more people want those jobs, say 1,100, because the pay is better. The gap of 1,100 - 900 = 200 is a surplus of labor, which in a labor market has another name: unemployment. The 900 who keep their jobs earn $3 more an hour. The 100 who lose a job, and the 100 new job seekers who cannot find one, are worse off.

That is the model. The debate is about how big the numbers really are. Critics of a high minimum wage argue that job losses fall hardest on teenagers and workers with the least experience, that employers respond with fewer hours and higher prices, and that a large jump speeds up automation. Supporters argue that many employers have few competitors for local workers and were paying less than workers were worth, so a moderate floor can raise pay with little job loss. They also point to studies of neighboring states with different minimums that found small employment effects. Both sides agree on one thing: a floor set far above the market wage, say $40 an hour, would destroy many jobs. The disagreement is about moderate increases, and the evidence is genuinely mixed.

words.d: the market where households sell hours of work and employers buy them; the wage is the price
a legal floor under the hourly wage; the federal rate has been $7.25 since 2009
a surplus of labor: people willing to work at the going wage who cannot find a job
replacing human work with machines or software, more attractive to employers when wages rise

look.title: A Diner Owner Does the Math
look.text: Rosa runs a diner with six servers earning $12 an hour. The state minimum rises to $15. Her payroll goes up 25%. She considers three responses: raise menu prices about 8%, cut one server and buy two tablet ordering stands, or keep everything the same and accept a smaller profit. Her regulars are mostly retirees on fixed incomes.
look.prompt: Work out what each choice means for Rosa, her servers and her customers. Which one does the simple model predict, and what real-world facts might push her toward a different answer?

check.q: In the town example, a $15 floor leads employers to hire 900 workers while 1,100 want jobs. What is the 200-worker gap called?
check.why: In a labor market, quantity supplied above quantity demanded is a surplus of workers, which is unemployment. 1,100 - 900 = 200.

check.q: Which of these is an argument made by SUPPORTERS of a moderate minimum wage increase?
choices: It causes teenagers to lose jobs
Employers with few local competitors were paying less than workers were worth, so a floor can raise pay with little job loss
check.why: That is the market-power argument used by supporters. The other three are arguments made by critics.

check.q: In a labor market, who is on the demand side?
choices: Employers, who buy hours of work
check.why: Employers demand labor and households supply it. The wage is the price that matches them.

lessons.title: Farm Price Supports
lessons.mainIdea: When the government guarantees a crop price above the market, it must buy or store the surplus, and taxpayers pay for it.
reading: Illinois is one of the nation's largest producers of corn and soybeans, so farm prices matter here. Since the 1930s the federal government has used many programs to hold up crop prices, starting with the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933. One classic tool is a *price support*: the government promises to buy a crop at a set price, which acts as a floor. If the market price falls below the support, farmers sell to the government instead.

Here is a labeled example. Suppose wheat would clear at $4 a bushel with 100 million bushels traded. The government sets a support price of $5. At $5, farmers grow 110 million bushels, but millers and bakers buy only 90 million. The surplus is 110 - 90 = 20 million bushels, and the government has promised to buy it. The bill is 20 million × $5 = $100 million, paid by taxpayers. Then the wheat has to be stored, given away or sold abroad, and each choice has its own cost. Consumers also pay more at the bakery, because bread now uses $5 wheat instead of $4 wheat.

Supporters of farm supports argue that farm prices swing wildly with weather, that a bad year can wipe out a family farm, and that a steady food supply is a national interest. Critics reply that the biggest payments go to the largest farms, that the programs encourage growing crops nobody wants, and that direct insurance against bad harvests would protect farmers at lower cost. Today most U.S. farm programs use crop insurance and payments tied to low prices rather than government purchases, but the logic of the floor and the surplus is the same.

words.d: a government promise to buy a crop at a set minimum price, which works as a price floor
a unit of volume used for grain; wheat and corn prices are quoted per bushel
a policy that pays a farmer when a harvest or price falls short, instead of the government setting a floor

look.title: Wheat Under a $5 Support (labeled example)
look.cite: An invented wheat schedule built for this lesson.
look.prompt: At a $5 support, how many bushels must the government buy, and what does that cost? What would a $6 support cost?

check.q: With a $5 support, farmers grow 110 million bushels and buyers take 90 million. What does the government spend buying the surplus?
check.why: Surplus = 110 - 90 = 20 million bushels. 20 million × $5 = $100 million.

check.q: A price support raises the price of wheat from $4 to $5. Who besides taxpayers pays part of the cost?
choices: Consumers, who pay more for bread made from $5 wheat
check.why: The higher floor price is passed along in the price of flour and bread, so consumers pay more at the store.

check.q: Which is an argument CRITICS make against farm price supports?
choices: Supports lower the price of food
Farmers do not need steady prices
The biggest payments go to the largest farms and encourage growing crops nobody wants
check.why: Critics point to who receives the money and to the surplus the floor creates. Supporters answer with price swings and food security.

lessons.title: Rationing Without Prices
lessons.mainIdea: When a price cannot ration, something else will: waiting, lotteries, coupons or connections, each with its own costs.
reading: When a ceiling binds, more people want the good than can have it, and the price is not allowed to sort them out. So other rules take over. The oldest is first come, first served: a *queue*. It feels fair, but it rations by time instead of money, and time is a real cost. Suppose gas is $0.20 a gallon cheaper under a ceiling than it would be in a free market, and a driver buys 10 gallons after waiting two hours. She saved $2 and spent two hours doing it. That is a return of $1 an hour, far below what most people earn. The saving is real, but the hours are simply lost; no seller receives them.

A *lottery* rations by luck. It is cheap to run and hard to game, but it sends no signal and gives no reward for producing more. Concert tickets and some city housing programs use it. *Ration coupons* were the World War II approach: each family received a book of stamps for sugar, meat, gasoline and tires, and a purchase required both money and a stamp. Coupons can direct goods to everyone equally, but they take a large bureaucracy and invite trading and forgery.

The least fair method is favoritism. When a landlord has forty applicants for one controlled apartment, he can pick his cousin, or the applicant who slips him cash, or the one whose last name he likes. Rationing by connections rewards who you know instead of what you offer. Notice that all four methods share a weakness the price system does not have. None of them tells producers to make more, and none rewards them for doing so. Non-price rationing divides the existing pie; only price grows it.

words.d: a waiting line; rationing by queue gives the good to whoever is willing to wait longest
rationing by random draw; fair in one sense, but it sends no signal to producers
a government-issued stamp required in addition to money to buy a rationed good, used in World War II
rationing by personal connection or bribe, which rewards who you know

look.title: Four Ways to Hand Out 100 Tickets
look.text: A school has 100 seats for a championship game and 400 students who want one. The principal considers: (1) sell them at whatever price fills exactly 100 seats, (2) first 100 in line at 6 a.m., (3) a random drawing, (4) let each teacher pick a few students. Some students have jobs in the morning; some have money; some have a teacher who likes them.
look.prompt: For each method, who tends to get a seat and what does it cost them? Which method is fairest, and does your answer change if the school could add seats when tickets sell for a lot?

check.q: A driver waits two hours to buy 10 gallons at a controlled price $0.20 below the market price. What did the wait earn her per hour?
check.why: She saved 10 × $0.20 = $2 over two hours, which is $1 an hour. The hours went to nobody.

check.q: Which rationing method requires both money and a government stamp to make a purchase?
check.why: Under World War II coupon rationing, a buyer needed cash plus a stamp from a ration book.

check.q: What weakness do all non-price rationing methods share compared with a market price?
choices: They do not signal or reward producers to make more
check.why: Queues, lotteries, coupons and favoritism only divide what already exists. A rising price also motivates more supply.

lessons.title: Black Markets
lessons.mainIdea: A binding price control pushes trades outside the law, where prices are higher, quality is unchecked and buyers have no protection.
reading: Go back to the used bikes with a $150 ceiling and a 20-bike shortage. A student who badly needs a bike and a seller who badly wants more than $150 can both do better by breaking the rule. They meet in a parking lot; the student pays $260 in cash, more than the old $200 equilibrium, and the seller hands over the bike with no receipt. That trade is part of a *black market*: buying and selling at a price the law forbids.

Why $260 and not $200? Because the legal market has soaked up 50 bikes at $150, and the buyers left over are competing for whatever leaks out from under the ceiling. Sellers also charge extra for the risk of getting caught. Black-market prices under a ceiling are usually above the old free-market price, not below it. The control that was meant to make bikes cheaper has made some of them more expensive.

Black markets appear under floors too. A worker who cannot find a job at the $15 minimum may agree to work for $10 in cash, off the books. Both sides break the law, and the worker gives up every legal protection: no record of hours, no unemployment insurance, no recourse if the boss refuses to pay. Rent-controlled cities see key fees and unofficial sublets at double the legal rent. Ticket ceilings produce scalpers outside the arena. The pattern is always the same: a gap between the legal price and the price people would actually agree on, and someone willing to fill it for a fee.

words.d: buying and selling at prices or in ways the law forbids, usually where a control binds
work paid in cash and not reported, often to get around a minimum wage or taxes
someone who resells tickets above the legal or face price

look.title: The Parking-Lot Price
look.text: A town caps concert tickets at $50 to keep them affordable. At $50 the 5,000-seat arena sells out in four minutes, and 15,000 fans are left without tickets. Outside on show night, tickets change hands for $180. The arena had planned a second night if ticket sales showed strong demand, but at $50 it cannot tell how strong demand really is.
look.prompt: Explain why the resale price is above what a free market price would probably have been. What did the cap do to the arena's decision about a second night?

check.q: Under a $150 ceiling, a bike that used to clear at $200 sells in a parking lot for $260. Why is the black-market price above $200?
choices: The seller is confused about the law
Bikes became more expensive to make
The leftover buyers compete for the few bikes that leak out, and sellers charge for the risk
check.why: The legal market absorbs some supply at $150, and the remaining buyers bid up whatever is left. Risk adds a premium on top.

check.q: Which of these is a black market caused by a price FLOOR?
choices: Paying a worker $10 cash off the books when the minimum is $15
Paying a $3,000 key fee for a rent-controlled apartment
check.why: The minimum wage is a floor. The other examples involve ceilings (tickets, rent) or non-price rationing (the line).

check.q: What does a worker paid off the books give up?
choices: Legal protections such as a record of hours and unemployment insurance
Nothing; it is the same as a regular job
The chance to be paid in cash
check.why: Off-the-books work has no legal record, so the worker cannot claim benefits or force the boss to pay what was promised.

lessons.title: Taxes, Subsidies and Who Pays
lessons.mainIdea: Whoever the law names to pay a tax, the real burden is shared by buyers and sellers, and it falls more heavily on whichever side is less able to walk away.
reading: Suppose a state adds a *tax* of $1 per gallon on gasoline and requires stations to send the money in. Students often assume the station pays the whole dollar. Watch what actually happens in a labeled example. Before the tax, gas sells for $3.00. Stations now need $1 more per gallon to earn what they earned before, so they try to raise the price. But at $4.00 some drivers cut back, so stations cannot pass the whole dollar through. The price settles at $3.60. Drivers pay $0.60 more than before. Stations collect $3.60, send $1 to the state and keep $2.60, which is $0.40 less than before. The dollar is split: 60 cents on buyers, 40 cents on sellers.

Economists call this split the *incidence* of the tax. The rule is simple. The side that can least escape the market bears more of the tax. Drivers cannot easily stop buying gas to get to work, so their demand is relatively inelastic and they carry the larger share. If demand for a good were very elastic, meaning buyers would abandon it at the first price increase, sellers would have to absorb most of the tax instead. The name on the tax form does not decide who pays. The elasticities do.

A *subsidy* is a tax in reverse: the government pays money per unit instead of collecting it. If the state paid $1 per gallon to stations, the price would not fall by a full dollar. In the same market it might fall by $0.60 to $2.40, with drivers gaining 60 cents and stations keeping the other 40 cents. Again the less elastic side, the one that would keep buying anyway, captures the larger share. This is why a subsidy meant for buyers can end up largely in sellers' pockets, and why economists always ask who really pays rather than who writes the check.

words.d: a required payment to the government; a per-unit tax adds a set amount to each item sold
who actually bears the cost of a tax after prices adjust, as opposed to who sends the payment
a government payment per unit of a good, the opposite of a tax
very responsive to price; the more elastic side of a market escapes more of a tax

look.title: Who Pays the Soda Tax?
look.text: A city puts a tax of 10 cents per can on soda, collected from stores. In one neighborhood, the price of a can rises from $1.00 to $1.08. In another, where shoppers can drive five minutes to a store outside the city limits, the price rises only to $1.03.
look.prompt: In each neighborhood, how much of the 10 cents do shoppers pay and how much do stores absorb? Why does the split differ? Use the word elastic in your answer.

check.q: A $1 tax on gasoline is collected from stations. The price rises from $3.00 to $3.60. How much of the tax do drivers bear per gallon?
check.why: Drivers pay $3.60 - $3.00 = $0.60 more than before. Stations bear the remaining $0.40.

check.q: Which side of a market bears the larger share of a tax?
choices: Always the sellers, because they send in the money
The side that is less able to leave the market (less elastic)
check.why: Incidence depends on elasticity, not on who writes the check. The side that keeps trading despite the price change carries more of the burden.

check.q: The state pays a $1 per gallon subsidy to gas stations. The price falls from $3.00 to $2.40. How much of the subsidy do stations keep?
check.why: Drivers gain $0.60 of the dollar through the lower price. Stations keep the other $1.00 - $0.60 = $0.40.

review.q: A market for tutoring clears at $30 an hour. The school sets a maximum tutoring rate of $20. What is the most likely result?
choices: No change, because the cap is above equilibrium
review.why: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding. At $20, more students want tutoring and fewer tutors offer it, so there is a shortage.

review.q: Which of these price controls is NON-binding?
choices: A rent ceiling of $1,000 when the market rent is $1,500
A wage floor of $15 when the market wage is $12
A price floor of $2 on milk when the market price is $3
A ticket ceiling of $50 when the market price is $180
review.why: A floor binds only from above. A $2 floor under a $3 market price changes nothing. The other three all bind.

review.q: Under a price support, the government buys a surplus of 20 million bushels at $5 each. What does it spend?
Which job of a price is missing under every form of non-price rationing?
review.why: Queues, lotteries, coupons and favoritism all divide the existing supply, but none rewards producers for making more.

review.q: In the simple labor-market model, what does a minimum wage set above the market wage create?
choices: A surplus of workers, meaning unemployment
Higher wages for every worker with no other effect
review.why: A floor above equilibrium raises quantity supplied and lowers quantity demanded. The gap is unemployed workers.

review.q: Gasoline lines in the 1970s are best described as:
choices: Proof that oil had run out
A surplus caused by a price floor
A shortage caused by a price ceiling on top of real scarcity
A normal feature of any oil market
review.why: Oil supply fell, but the lines came from a legal price held below the new equilibrium. When the ceiling was removed, the lines ended.

review.q: A tax of $2 per item is collected from sellers. The price buyers pay rises from $10 to $11.50. Who bears more of the tax, and how much?
review.why: Buyers pay $1.50 more; sellers absorb the other $0.50. Buyers bear more, which means demand is the less elastic side here.

review.q: Why do black-market prices under a ceiling usually end up ABOVE the old free-market price?
choices: Leftover buyers compete for the few units that leak out, and sellers charge for the risk
Demand falls when a ceiling is imposed
review.why: The legal market takes some supply at the capped price. The remaining buyers bid up what is left, plus a premium for illegality.

chapters.title: Externalities and Public Goods
chapters.bigQuestion: If markets are so good at matching buyers and sellers, why do we still get polluted rivers, empty fisheries and crowded roads?

story.title: The Bill Nobody Sent
story.kicker: A paper mill, a river, and a town twenty miles downstream that never signed a contract with anyone.
paragraphs: Riverton is an invented town, but every piece of its story has happened somewhere in Illinois. In 1958 a paper mill opened on the river above the town. It hired 400 people, paid well and sold paper at a price that beat every competitor in the state. The mill's owners were proud of their low costs. They had a clean, modern plant, cheap wood from nearby forests, and a river that carried their waste water away for free.

That last word matters. For free. Every ton of paper the mill made sent bleach and pulp into the river. The river carried it down to Riverton, where people fished, swam and drew drinking water. Within ten years the fish were gone. The town had to build a filtration plant that cost $2 million and raised every water bill. A summer camp on the riverbank closed. Doctors noticed more stomach illness in children who swam.

Add it up and the mill was costing Riverton something like $4 for every ton of paper it made. But that $4 never showed up on the mill's books. The mill paid for wood, workers, electricity and machines. It did not pay for fish, water treatment or sick children, because nobody sent it a bill. Its price of paper, and the amount of paper it made, were based on costs that left out the town entirely.

The mill's owners were not villains. They were doing exactly what a market told them to do: keep costs down, sell more, and make a profit. The market simply had no way to charge them for the damage. A cost that lands on someone outside the deal is what economists call an externality, and it is one of the main reasons that a market, left completely alone, can produce the wrong amount of something.

Riverton's story has several possible endings. The town could sue. The state could cap what the mill dumps. The state could charge the mill $4 a ton for what it sends downstream. Or the town could pay the mill to clean up. Each ending is a real tool that governments use, and each has costs of its own. This chapter is about when markets fail, and what can be done about it.
story.think: The mill paid for wood and workers but not for the river. Who ended up paying for the river instead, and why did the market not send the mill a bill?

lessons.title: What Market Failure Means
lessons.mainIdea: A market fails when prices leave out a cost or benefit, so buyers and sellers produce too much or too little of something.
reading: In the last chapters, a free market price did three jobs well: it signaled, it rationed and it motivated. Underneath that success was a quiet assumption. The price of a good was supposed to reflect everything it cost to make and everything it was worth to have. When that assumption holds, the market amount is the right amount. Every unit that is worth more than it costs gets made, and nothing else does.

A *market failure* is a situation where that assumption breaks. The price of paper from the Riverton mill included wood and labor but not the poisoned river. The price was too low, so the mill sold too much paper. In other cases the price leaves out a benefit instead. A flu shot protects the person who gets it and also everyone she would have infected, but she pays for only her own protection, so too few people get the shot. Market failure does not mean the market collapsed. It means the market worked exactly as designed and still arrived at the wrong amount.

This chapter covers four main causes. *Externalities* are costs or benefits that spill onto people outside the transaction. *Public goods* are things like national defense that a market will not provide because nobody can be made to pay for them. *Common resources*, like fish in a lake, get overused because nobody owns them. And *imperfect information* lets one side of a deal know something the other side does not. For each one, you will see the failure in numbers first, then the standard tools governments use to repair it, and then the limits of those tools.

words.d: a situation where a market, working normally, produces too much or too little of a good because the price leaves something out
a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on someone who was not part of it
a good that one person's use does not reduce and that nobody can be kept from using, such as national defense
a resource nobody owns and everyone can use, such as fish in the open ocean
a situation in which one side of a trade knows more than the other

look.title: Sort the Failures
look.text: Four scenes: a neighbor's late-night music keeps you awake; nobody wants to pay for a new streetlight on a dark block even though everyone wants it; a used-car seller knows the transmission is failing and the buyer does not; a public pasture is grazed down to dirt because every rancher adds one more cow.
look.prompt: Match each scene to one of the four causes of market failure. In each case, what is the price leaving out?

check.q: What does it mean when economists say a market has failed?
choices: The market produced the wrong amount because the price left out a cost or benefit
No one is buying or selling
check.why: Market failure is about the quantity being wrong, not about the market stopping. The price is missing something.

check.q: A flu shot also protects the people the patient would have infected, but she pays only for her own protection. What is the likely result?
choices: Too many people get flu shots
Too few people get flu shots
Exactly the right number get flu shots
The price of flu shots rises to infinity
check.why: When a benefit spills onto others and is not counted in the price, buyers undervalue the good and the market produces too little of it.

check.q: Fish in a lake that anyone may catch are an example of which cause of market failure?
check.why: A common resource is unowned and open to all, so each user ignores the cost to everyone else. That leads to overuse.

lessons.title: Costs That Land on Others
lessons.mainIdea: A negative externality makes the market produce too much, because the seller's cost is lower than the true cost to society.
reading: Put numbers on the Riverton mill. Suppose it costs the mill $10 to make a ton of paper, counting wood, labor and machines. That is the mill's *private cost*. Each ton also does about $4 of damage to the town downstream. That $4 is an *external cost*, because it falls on people outside the deal. The full cost to everyone, $10 + $4 = $14, is the *social cost*. The mill sees only the $10, so it happily sells paper for $12 and makes 1,000 tons a week. From society's view, each of those tons costs $14 and sells for $12; the mill is producing tons that are worth less than they truly cost.

Now think about the supply curve. The mill's supply curve is built from its $10 private cost. If the mill had to pay the $4 too, its supply curve would sit $4 higher at every quantity. At that higher curve, fewer tons are worth making. Suppose the mill would make only 700 tons a week if it faced the full $14. Then the market, left alone, produces 300 tons too many, and each of those 300 tons hurts the town more than it helps anyone. That gap is the size of the market failure.

The classic examples of *negative externalities* all fit this shape: smoke from a power plant, noise from an airport, traffic from one more car on a crowded highway, a neighbor's untreated yard spreading weeds. In every case the producer sees a cost that is too low, so the quantity is too high. Notice that the goal is not zero. Riverton would not want the mill closed; 400 jobs and paper at $12 are real benefits. The goal is the amount the town would choose if it were paying the full cost, which in this example is 700 tons, not 1,000 and not 0.

words.d: the cost a producer actually pays, such as wood, labor and machines
a cost of production that falls on someone outside the transaction, such as pollution damage
private cost plus external cost; the full cost to everyone
a cost spilling onto third parties, which leads a market to produce too much

look.title: The Mill's Costs Per Ton (labeled example)
look.cite: An invented cost table for the Riverton mill, built for this lesson.
look.prompt: From the mill's view, does a ton of paper earn a profit? From the town's view, is a ton worth what it costs? Explain the gap.

check.q: The mill's private cost is $10 a ton and the damage downstream is $4 a ton. What is the social cost?
check.why: Social cost = private cost + external cost = $10 + $4 = $14.

check.q: Because the mill ignores the $4 external cost, what does the market do?
check.why: A cost left out of the price makes supply look cheaper than it is, so quantity is higher than the social optimum. Here 1,000 tons instead of 700.

check.q: If the mill had to pay the full social cost, what would happen to its supply curve?
choices: It would shift to the right
It would shift up by $4 at every quantity
check.why: Adding $4 to the cost of each ton raises the price the mill needs at every quantity, which is an upward (leftward) shift of supply.

lessons.title: Benefits That Spill Over
lessons.mainIdea: A positive externality makes the market produce too little, because buyers count only their own benefit and not the benefit to others.
reading: A flu shot at a Chicago pharmacy costs $30. Suppose Jamal figures the shot is worth about $25 to him: fewer sick days, less misery. He skips it. But Jamal rides the Blue Line every day. If he catches the flu, he will probably pass it to two or three riders, and each of them may pass it on. The protection his shot gives to strangers is worth something like $15. The shot's *social benefit* is $25 + $15 = $40, which is more than the $30 price. Society would want Jamal vaccinated. Jamal, counting only his own $25, says no.

This is a *positive externality*: a benefit that spills onto people outside the deal. Because buyers weigh only their *private benefit*, demand is too low and the market produces too little. The mirror image of the mill: there, the supply curve was too low because of a hidden cost; here, the demand curve is too low because of a hidden benefit. Education is the biggest example. A student who finishes high school earns more, which is her private benefit. She also becomes a more informed voter, a more productive coworker and a less likely user of public aid, which benefits everyone else. That spillover is the standard economic case for public schools.

The standard fix runs in reverse from a tax. If the state pays $10 of Jamal's shot, the price to him falls to $20, below his $25 private benefit, and he gets vaccinated. The state has used a *subsidy* to add the external benefit back into his decision. Public subsidies for vaccines, K–12 schooling, college grants and research all rest on this logic. The open question is always the size of the spillover. If the external benefit of a good is small, the subsidy mostly rewards people for what they would have done anyway.

words.d: a benefit spilling onto third parties, which leads a market to produce too little
the value a buyer gets for herself from a good
private benefit plus the benefit to everyone else; the full value to society
a government payment that lowers the price of a good to encourage more of it

look.title: The Front Yard
look.text: Ms. Okafor spends $600 and many weekends planting flowers in her front yard. Her neighbors enjoy the view every day and one of them sells a house for $2,000 more than expected because the block looks cared for. Ms. Okafor did not get a cent of that $2,000.
look.prompt: Identify the private benefit and the external benefit. Would the neighborhood want more or fewer yards like hers than the market produces? What might a neighborhood association do about it?

check.q: Jamal values a flu shot at $25 for himself, and it protects others by $15. What is the social benefit?
check.why: Social benefit = private benefit + external benefit = $25 + $15 = $40.

check.q: Why does a market produce too little of a good with a positive externality?
choices: Buyers count only their own benefit, so demand is lower than the true value to society
check.why: The demand curve reflects private benefit only. The spillover benefit is missing, so quantity is below the social optimum.

check.q: A $10 subsidy lowers the shot's price from $30 to $20. Why does Jamal now buy it?
choices: The subsidy raised his private benefit
The subsidy made the shot free
check.why: He buys when the price he pays is below what the shot is worth to him. $20 is less than $25, so he says yes.

lessons.title: Taxes, Rules and Lawsuits
lessons.mainIdea: Governments correct externalities with taxes that put the missing cost into the price, with regulations that set limits, or with courts that enforce property rights.
reading: Back to Riverton. The state has three classic tools. The first is a *corrective tax*: charge the mill exactly the external cost, $4 per ton. Now the mill's cost is $14, the same as the social cost. It cuts output from 1,000 tons to 700 on its own, because the last 300 tons no longer pay. Nobody had to tell the mill how much to make; the price did the work. The tax also raises money, in this case 700 × $4 = $2,800 a week, which could help pay for Riverton's water plant. Economists tend to like corrective taxes because they let each polluter find its own cheapest way to cut back.

The second tool is *regulation*: a rule that says the mill may dump no more than a set amount, or must install a filter. Rules are simple to understand and to enforce, and they work even when the state cannot measure the damage in dollars. Their weakness is that one rule fits everyone. A mill that could cut pollution cheaply and one that could only cut it at great expense face the same requirement, so the total cleanup costs more than it needs to. Rules also give no reward for doing better than the limit.

The third tool is the courts. If Riverton owns the right to clean water, it can sue the mill for damages, and the threat of paying $4 a ton has the same effect as the tax. Sometimes the two sides can simply bargain: the town might pay the mill to install a filter if that is cheaper than a lawsuit, or the mill might pay the town for the right to dump a limited amount. Bargaining works well when the parties are few and the harm is clear. It works badly when thousands of people are affected and the cost of getting them all to agree is enormous, which is why air pollution across a whole city is usually handled by taxes or rules instead.

words.d: a tax set equal to the external cost of a good, so the price includes the harm to others
a government rule that limits how much of something may be produced or how it must be done
a legally enforced claim to use something and to keep others from harming it
money a court orders one party to pay another for harm done

look.title: Three Fixes for One Mill
look.text: The Riverton council must choose: (a) a $4 per ton tax on the mill, (b) a rule capping the mill's discharge at the level that comes with 700 tons, or (c) suing the mill for $4,000 a week in damages. The mill's engineers say they could cut pollution in half for $1 a ton with a new filter, but the rule would not reward them for going further.
look.prompt: Which fix gets the mill to 700 tons? Which one gives it a reason to install the $1 filter? Which raises money for the town's water plant? What are the drawbacks of each?

check.q: A corrective tax of $4 a ton is placed on the mill. What does it do to the mill's cost per ton?
choices: Raises it to $14, equal to the social cost
check.why: $10 private cost + $4 tax = $14, which matches the true cost to society. The mill then cuts output on its own.

check.q: After the tax, the mill makes 700 tons a week. How much tax revenue does the state collect weekly?
check.why: 700 tons × $4 per ton = $2,800.

check.q: What is the main weakness of a one-size-fits-all pollution rule compared with a tax?
choices: It makes all firms cut the same amount even when some could cut far more cheaply, so total cleanup costs more
check.why: A tax lets each firm find its cheapest cut; a uniform rule ignores those differences and gives no reward for beating the limit.

lessons.title: Tradable Permits
lessons.mainIdea: A cap-and-trade system fixes the total amount of pollution and lets firms buy and sell the right to pollute, so cleanup happens where it is cheapest.
reading: Suppose two power plants each emit 100 tons of a pollutant a year, and the state wants the total cut from 200 tons to 120. It could order each plant to cut 40 tons. But the plants are different. Plant A has an old boiler and can remove a ton for $200. Plant B is already modern and can remove a ton only at $500. Equal cuts cost A 40 × $200 = $8,000 and B 40 × $500 = $20,000, a total of $28,000.

Now try *cap and trade*. The state prints 120 *permits*, each allowing one ton, and gives 60 to each plant. A plant may emit only as many tons as it holds permits, but permits can be bought and sold. Plant B looks at its $500 per ton cleanup cost and would rather buy permits. Plant A can clean up for $200 and would rather sell. Suppose they agree on a price of $300 per permit. A cuts all the way to 20 tons, removing 80 tons at $200 each, which costs $16,000, and sells its 40 spare permits to B for $12,000. A's net cost is $4,000. B cuts nothing and spends $12,000 on permits. The total real cleanup cost is $16,000, not $28,000, and the state still gets exactly 120 tons.

That is the whole appeal. The *cap* sets the total; the *trade* finds the cheapest way to hit it. Firms that can clean up cheaply profit by doing extra, and firms that cannot pay them to do it. The United States used this design in the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments to cut sulfur dioxide, the main cause of acid rain, from power plants, and emissions fell well below the cap at lower cost than many had predicted. Critics worry about who gets the permits for free, about firms gaming the market, and about pollution concentrating near plants that buy permits. Supporters answer that the cap is a hard number, which a tax cannot promise.

words.d: a system that limits total pollution and lets firms buy and sell permits to pollute
a legal right to emit one unit of a pollutant, which can be bought and sold under cap and trade
the fixed total amount of pollution allowed, equal to the number of permits issued

look.title: Two Plants, One Cap (labeled example)
rows: Plant A cleanup cost per ton
Plant B cleanup cost per ton
With trading at $300: total real cleanup cost
Plant A net cost after selling permits
Plant B cost of buying 40 permits
look.cite: An invented two-plant example built for this lesson.
look.prompt: Why is Plant B willing to pay $300 for a permit? Why is Plant A willing to sell at $300? Who is better off than under equal cuts?

check.q: Plant A can remove a ton for $200 and Plant B for $500. Under cap and trade, which plant does the cleanup and why?
choices: Plant A, because it is cheaper to cut there and it can sell spare permits
Plant B, because it is more modern
Both cut equally, as the law requires
Neither; permits eliminate the need to cut
check.why: Trading moves cleanup to the low-cost plant. A cuts extra and sells permits; B buys them instead of paying $500 a ton.

check.q: Equal cuts cost $28,000. With trading, real cleanup costs $16,000. How much does society save?
check.why: $28,000 - $16,000 = $12,000 saved, with the same 120 tons of pollution.

check.q: What advantage do supporters claim for a cap over a corrective tax?
choices: A cap is easier to calculate
The cap guarantees a fixed total amount of pollution, which a tax cannot promise
check.why: A tax fixes the price and lets quantity vary; a cap fixes the quantity and lets the permit price vary.

lessons.title: Non-Rival and Non-Excludable
lessons.mainIdea: A public good is one that many can use at once and that no one can be kept from using, which is why private sellers cannot make money providing it.
reading: A slice of pizza is a private good. If you eat it, nobody else can, and a shop can keep you from taking it until you pay. Economists say pizza is *rival* and *excludable*. National defense is the opposite. When the country is protected from attack, one more person living in it is protected too, at no extra cost: defense is *non-rival*. And there is no way to protect the country while leaving out the family that refused to chip in: defense is *non-excludable*. A good with both properties is a *public good*.

Think about a lighthouse in the 1800s, the textbook example. Its beam warns every ship that passes, so one ship's use of the light does not use it up. And the keeper cannot switch the beam off for ships that did not pay. A private company that built a lighthouse and tried to charge would find captains simply using the light and sailing on. So no company builds one, even though the ships together would gladly pay far more than it costs. That is the market failure: a valuable good that no seller can profit from. In practice, governments built and ran most lighthouses.

Most goods are somewhere between pure private and pure public. A city street is non-excludable but becomes rival when it is jammed. Cable TV is non-rival but excludable, because the company can scramble the signal for non-payers. The pure public goods that markets truly cannot supply are a short list: defense, basic scientific research, clean air, the court system, flood control, and knowledge such as a weather forecast that anyone can hear on the radio. For these, the standard answer is for the government to provide them and pay through taxes, which is a way of forcing everyone who benefits to contribute.

words.d: a good is rival when one person's use leaves less for others, like a slice of pizza
a good is excludable when a seller can keep non-payers from using it
one person's use does not reduce what is left for others, like a lighthouse beam
there is no practical way to keep non-payers from using the good
a good that is both non-rival and non-excludable, such as national defense

look.title: Smith on Public Works
look.text: Adam Smith wrote that a government's third duty is to build and keep up public institutions and public works that benefit a whole society greatly, but whose profit could never repay any individual or small group, so that no individual or small group could be expected to build or maintain them.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book V, 1776 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Smith was no friend of big government. Why did even he think some things must be built by the state? Use the words non-rival and non-excludable in your answer.

check.q: Which good is BOTH non-rival and non-excludable?
check.why: Protecting one more resident costs nothing extra and nobody can be left out. Pizza is rival and excludable; cable is excludable; a crowded road is rival.

check.q: Why would a private company not build a lighthouse in the 1800s?
choices: Ships could use the light without paying, so the company could not earn back its cost
Lighthouses were too expensive to build
check.why: Non-excludability means non-payers benefit anyway. With no way to charge, no seller can profit, even though the good is valuable.

check.q: Cable TV is non-rival but a company can scramble the signal for non-payers. Which statement is correct?
choices: Cable TV is a pure public good
Cable TV is excludable, so a private company can sell it
Cable TV cannot be provided by anyone
check.why: Excludability lets a seller collect payment. A good that is only non-rival can still be sold profitably.

lessons.title: The Free-Rider Problem
lessons.mainIdea: When people can enjoy a good without paying, many will not pay, and the good goes underprovided unless everyone is required to contribute.
reading: A neighborhood of 1,000 homes wants a Fourth of July fireworks show that costs $5,000. Ask each household what the show is worth to them, and suppose the honest average answer is $10. The show is worth $10,000 to the neighborhood and costs $5,000, so it clearly should happen. A volunteer goes door to door collecting $5 from each home. Here is what she hears: 'I would love to see it, but I am a little short this month. You will get enough from the others.' She collects $1,800. No show.

Every household that answered that way was being a *free rider*. Fireworks light the whole sky; a family that pays nothing sees exactly the same show as one that paid $5. So each family's best move, thinking only of itself, is to let the neighbors pay. When everyone reasons the same way, the show does not happen and every family loses $10 of enjoyment to save $5. The free-rider problem is the reason public goods fail in the market: the goods are non-excludable, so voluntary payment falls short.

The usual solution is to replace voluntary payment with a required one. A town council can put $5 on every property tax bill and fund the show, which is what happens with roads, police, courts and defense. Taxes are, in this sense, the price of public goods, collected from everyone because everyone benefits. Voluntary methods work too for small groups where people know each other, and charities and public broadcasting survive on donors who choose not to free ride. But the larger the group, the easier it is to hide, and the more a public good depends on a required payment.

words.d: someone who enjoys a good without paying for it, because they cannot be kept out
a contribution people choose to make, which usually falls short for a non-excludable good
a tax or fee everyone must pay, used to fund goods that free riding would otherwise starve

look.title: The Group Project
look.text: Five students share one grade on a group project. Two do most of the work. Two do a little. One does nothing and gets the same A. The next semester, the two hard workers decide to do less, because why should they carry everyone? The project quality collapses.
look.prompt: Who is the free rider? Why did the problem get worse over time? What could a teacher change so that each student's payment, their effort, is no longer voluntary?

check.q: A fireworks show is worth $10 to each of 1,000 homes and costs $5,000. Voluntary collection brings in $1,800. What happened?
choices: The show was not worth doing
The show cost more than its value
Many households free rode, expecting others to pay for a show they could not be kept from seeing
check.why: The show is worth $10,000 against a $5,000 cost, so it should happen. Non-excludability let households benefit without paying.

check.q: Why is free riding especially a problem for public goods?
choices: Public goods are non-excludable, so non-payers get the same benefit as payers
check.why: If you cannot be kept out, paying gains you nothing extra. So many people choose not to pay.

check.q: What is the standard way governments overcome free riding for goods like roads and defense?
choices: Fund them through required taxes that everyone pays
check.why: A required payment replaces the voluntary one that free riding undermines. Taxes are the price of public goods.

lessons.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
lessons.mainIdea: A resource that anyone may use and nobody owns gets overused, because each user ignores the cost their use imposes on everyone else.
reading: A lake holds a fish population that anyone may catch. Here is a labeled example of what happens as boats are added. One boat catches 100 fish a week. Two boats together catch 180, so 90 each. Three catch 240 total, 80 each. Four catch 280, 70 each. Five catch 300, 60 each. Six still catch 300, 50 each. Every extra boat crowds the others and thins the fish, so the total grows more slowly and then stops. Suppose it costs the equivalent of 55 fish a week to run a boat.

Look at the choice from one fisher's point of view. He asks whether his boat's catch beats 55. With five boats, each gets 60, which beats 55, so a fifth boat goes out. A sixth would get only 50, so it stays home. The lake ends up with five boats. Now look at it from the lake's point of view. The third boat raised the total from 180 to 240, adding 60 fish, more than its 55 cost. The fourth added only 40 fish, and the fifth added 20.
