Those last two boats each cost 55 and added less than that. They were profitable to their owners only because they took fish away from the boats already there. The lake would be best off with three boats. Open access gave it five.

The biologist Garrett Hardin named this pattern the *tragedy of the commons* in 1968. The same logic empties ocean fisheries, cuts down shared forests, crowds highways and overpumps groundwater. It is a negative externality with a twist: the victims and the polluters are the same group of people. The fixes are the ones you already know. Assign *property rights*, so an owner has a reason to protect the resource. Limit access with quotas, licenses or seasons, which is what fishing regulators do. Or charge a fee for use, like a toll on a crowded road. Each turns an unowned resource into one that somebody has a reason to keep.

words.d: the overuse of a resource that everyone can use and nobody owns, named by Garrett Hardin in 1968
a resource anyone may use with no owner and no limit
a legal limit on how much of a resource each user may take
an enforced claim of ownership, which gives the owner a reason to protect a resource

look.title: Boats on One Lake (labeled example)
look.cite: An invented catch table for one lake, built for this lesson. Running a boat costs the equivalent of 55 fish.
look.prompt: For each added boat, compute how many fish it adds to the total. Which boats add more than 55? Why do five boats go out anyway?

check.q: Four boats catch 280 fish and five boats catch 300. How many fish does the fifth boat ADD to the lake's total?
check.why: 300 - 280 = 20 fish. The fifth boat's own catch of 60 came mostly from fish the other boats would have caught.

check.q: If running a boat costs 55 fish, why does a fifth fisher still go out even though the boat adds only 20 to the total?
choices: He does not know how to count
He is required to by law
He plans to sell the boat
His own catch is 60, which beats 55; he ignores the 40 fish he takes from the others
check.why: Each user looks at his own catch, not the effect on everyone. The cost to the other boats is an externality he does not pay.

check.q: Which fix turns an open-access lake into a resource someone has a reason to protect?
choices: Giving one owner property rights or setting catch quotas
check.why: Ownership or quotas make users bear the cost of overuse. That is the standard remedy for a commons.

sections.title: Information and the Role of Government

lessons.title: When One Side Knows More
lessons.mainIdea: When sellers know more than buyers, buyers pay less for everything, the best goods leave the market, and quality collapses unless information can be shared.
reading: Suppose used cars of one model come in two kinds. A well-kept car is worth $10,000 and a badly kept one, a lemon, is worth $4,000. Half the cars on the lot are each kind. The seller knows which is which. The buyer cannot tell; both cars are shiny and the salesman says both are great. What should a buyer offer? If she cannot tell them apart, a car is worth about the average, $7,000, to her. So that is what buyers offer.

Now watch the owners of good cars. They know their car is worth $10,000 and they are being offered $7,000. Many refuse to sell. The owners of lemons, offered $7,000 for a $4,000 car, sell eagerly. So the cars that actually change hands are mostly lemons. Buyers learn this and lower their offers, which drives out even more good cars. In the extreme, only lemons trade, at $4,000, and everyone who owned a good car and wanted to sell it is stuck. The economist George Akerlof described this in 1970, and the idea won a Nobel Prize. It is called *adverse selection*: when one side knows more, the market attracts the worst goods.

The same problem appears in insurance, where the buyer knows more about her health than the insurer, and in hiring, where the worker knows more about his effort than the boss. The fixes all work by moving information across the gap. Warranties let a seller with a good car prove it, because a lemon seller cannot afford the repair promises. Inspections, vehicle history reports and reviews let buyers learn. Laws that require disclosure, from food labels to *lemon laws* for cars, force the informed side to share. Where information cannot be shared, markets shrink or vanish, which is why *imperfect information* counts as a market failure.

words.d: when one side of a trade knows more, the goods or people who show up to trade tend to be the worst ones
a used car with hidden defects; the classic example of a good whose quality only the seller knows
a seller's promise to repair or replace, which signals quality because a seller of a lemon cannot afford it
a state law that requires refunds or replacements for new cars with repeated serious defects

look.title: The Health Plan Nobody Healthy Buys
look.text: An insurer offers a plan at $400 a month, priced for the average person. The people who sign up are mostly those who expect big medical bills; healthy people think $400 is too much and skip it. The insurer loses money and raises the price to $600. Now even more healthy people drop out.
look.prompt: Explain how this is the used-car problem in a different costume. What could break the cycle? Think about who knows what, and about rules that require everyone to join.

check.q: Good cars are worth $10,000 and lemons $4,000, and buyers cannot tell them apart. If half are each kind, about what will a buyer offer?
check.why: With no way to tell, a car is worth the average: ($10,000 + $4,000) ÷ 2 = $7,000.

check.q: When buyers offer $7,000, what happens to the mix of cars offered for sale?
choices: Owners of good cars refuse to sell, so mostly lemons remain
Owners of lemons refuse to sell
check.why: $7,000 is below a good car's value and above a lemon's. Good cars leave the market and lemons stay. That is adverse selection.

check.q: Why does a warranty help solve the used-car problem?
choices: It lowers the price of every car
It forces buyers to pay more
A seller of a good car can afford the promise, while a seller of a lemon cannot, so the warranty signals quality
check.why: A warranty moves information across the gap. Only sellers who know their car is sound will offer to pay for repairs.

lessons.title: What Governments Do in a Market Economy
lessons.mainIdea: In a mixed economy, government sets the rules, provides public goods, corrects externalities, protects competition, aids the poor and steadies the whole economy.
reading: The United States has a *mixed economy*: markets make most decisions, and government does a set of jobs that markets do badly. Economists generally list six. First, the government defines and enforces *property rights* through courts, police and contract law. A market cannot work if you cannot be sure the bike you bought is yours. Second, it provides public goods: defense, courts, roads, basic research, weather forecasts. Third, it corrects externalities with the taxes, rules and permits from this chapter, including the Environmental Protection Agency's limits on air and water pollution.

Fourth, it protects competition. When one firm controls a market, it can raise prices and cut quality, so antitrust laws since the Sherman Act of 1890 have limited monopolies and blocked some mergers; the next unit takes this up in detail. Fifth, it redistributes income. A market pays people what their work is worth to buyers, which can be very little for the sick, the very young, the very old or the unlucky. Programs like Social Security, Medicaid and food assistance transfer income from those who have more to those who have less. Sixth, it stabilizes the economy, using taxes, spending and the Federal Reserve's control of interest rates to soften recessions and restrain inflation, which is the subject of the grade 11–12 course.

Every one of these jobs is paid for with taxes, and taxes have costs of their own. So each job invites a question about size: how much defense, how strict a pollution limit, how large a safety net. Those are questions that economics can inform but cannot settle, because they involve values as well as numbers. Economists can say what a policy will likely do to prices, jobs and output. Whether the trade-off is worth it is a question for voters.

words.d: an economy in which markets make most decisions and government provides rules, public goods and a safety net
laws, starting with the Sherman Act of 1890, that limit monopolies and protect competition
government transfers of income from those with more to those with less, through taxes and programs
government action to soften recessions and restrain inflation

look.title: A Day of Government Jobs
look.text: You wake up, check a weather forecast, drive on a paved road past a police car, buy lunch that was inspected for safety, pay sales tax, and read that two big grocery chains were blocked from merging. Your grandmother's Social Security check arrived the same morning. The Fed announced an interest rate decision at 1 p.m.
look.prompt: Match each event to one of the six jobs of government. Which of these could a market have handled on its own, and which could it not?

check.q: Which government job makes it possible for a market in bikes to work at all?
choices: Defining and enforcing property rights so buyers know what they own
check.why: Markets rest on ownership and enforceable contracts. Without them, nobody can safely buy or sell.

check.q: Social Security, Medicaid and food assistance are examples of which government role?
choices: Redistributing income to those the market pays little
check.why: These programs transfer income from those with more to those with less, which markets alone do not do.

check.q: Economists can predict what a stricter pollution limit will do to prices and jobs. What can economics NOT settle?
choices: Whether the limit will raise costs
Whether the trade-off is worth it, which depends on values and is a question for voters
check.why: Economics describes consequences. Choosing among them involves values, which is why the size of government is a political question.

lessons.title: The Limits of Government
lessons.mainIdea: Government can fail too: it lacks information, responds to lobbying and elections, and its rules can produce results nobody intended.
reading: A market failure shows that a market has produced the wrong amount. It does not prove that government will do better. Economists use the term *government failure* for the ways public action can also go wrong. The first is information. To set the Riverton tax at exactly $4, the state has to know the damage per ton. In real life the number is uncertain and contested, and a tax set at $1 or $9 gets the amount of paper wrong in the other direction. Markets pool the knowledge of millions of buyers and sellers in a price; a regulator has a staff and a budget.

The second is *incentives*. Officials respond to voters, and to organized groups more than to scattered ones. A subsidy that gives $100 million to 1,000 farms is worth fighting for if you are one of the farms, and not worth a letter if you are one of 300 million taxpayers paying 33 cents each. This is why *rent-seeking*, spending effort to win favors from government rather than to produce something, is a permanent feature of politics. Price controls from the last chapter often survive not because they work but because the people they help are visible and the people they hurt are not.

The third is unintended consequences. Rent control was meant to make housing affordable and shrank the housing supply. A rule requiring expensive safety gear on small businesses can push their work into the black market where there is no safety at all. None of this means government should do nothing about the mill or the lake. It means the comparison is never between an imperfect market and a perfect fix. It is between an imperfect market and an imperfect government, and the honest economist asks which imperfection is smaller in the case at hand.

words.d: when public action makes an outcome worse or fails to improve it, because of information limits, incentives or side effects
a reward or penalty that shapes what a person, firm or official decides to do
spending effort to win money or favors from government rather than to produce anything
a result of a policy that its makers did not plan and often did not want

look.title: The Sugar Program
look.text: Suppose a country limits sugar imports so its own growers get a higher price. A few thousand growers each gain tens of thousands of dollars a year and hire lobbyists to keep the program. Every consumer pays a few dollars more a year for candy and soda and never notices. Candy makers move some factories abroad, where sugar is cheaper.
look.prompt: Explain why this program survives even if the losses to consumers add up to more than the gains to growers. Which of the three kinds of government failure does it show?

check.q: Why is it hard for a regulator to set a corrective tax at exactly the right level?
choices: Regulators are not allowed to collect information
The regulator must know the exact damage per unit, which is uncertain and contested
check.why: A corrective tax works only if it equals the external cost. That number is hard to measure, so the tax can be too high or too low.

check.q: A subsidy gives $100 million to 1,000 farms and costs 300 million taxpayers 33 cents each. Why does it tend to survive?
choices: The farms have a strong reason to lobby while each taxpayer has almost none
check.why: Concentrated gains organize; scattered losses do not. That is the incentive problem behind rent-seeking.

check.q: What is the fair comparison when deciding whether government should act on a market failure?
choices: A perfect market versus a perfect government
An imperfect market versus an imperfect government
A perfect market versus an imperfect government
There is no comparison; government should always act
check.why: Both markets and governments can fail. The honest question is which imperfection is smaller in the specific case.

review.q: A trucking company's private cost per delivery is $50, and its trucks cause $8 of road wear and pollution per delivery paid by others. What is the social cost per delivery?
review.why: Social cost = private cost + external cost = $50 + $8 = $58.

review.q: Which of these is a positive externality?
choices: A homeowner's flower garden that raises neighbors' home values
review.why: The garden's benefit spills onto neighbors who did not pay for it. The other three are costs spilling onto others.

review.q: A corrective tax equal to the external cost is placed on a polluting good. What happens to the quantity produced?
choices: It falls to the amount society would choose if it paid the full cost
review.why: The tax puts the missing cost into the price, so producers cut back to the socially efficient level, not to zero.

review.q: Which good is non-excludable but becomes rival when crowded?
review.why: Anyone can use a street, but in a traffic jam each car reduces the space for others. Defense is non-rival; pizza and cable are excludable.

review.q: Why does voluntary payment for a public good usually fall short?
choices: People can benefit without paying, so many free ride
Public goods are illegal to sell
review.why: Non-excludability means non-payers get the same benefit. Each person's best private move is to let others pay.

review.q: In the lake example, the fourth boat catches 70 fish but raises the total catch from 240 to 280. A boat costs 55 fish. From the lake's point of view, should the fourth boat go out?
choices: No, because it adds only 40 fish, which is less than its 55 cost
No, because it catches fewer fish than the first boat
review.why: What matters to the lake is the boat's addition to the total: 280 - 240 = 40, which is below the 55 cost. The owner sees 70 because he takes fish from others.

review.q: Under cap and trade, Plant A can cut a ton for $200 and Plant B for $500. Permits sell for $300. What will each plant do?
choices: A cuts and sells permits; B buys permits instead of cutting
review.why: A profits by cutting at $200 and selling permits for $300. B saves by paying $300 for permits instead of $500 to cut.

review.q: Which of these is an example of GOVERNMENT failure rather than market failure?
choices: A rent-control law shrinks the supply of apartments
A used-car buyer cannot tell a good car from a lemon
Nobody pays for a fireworks show
review.why: Rent control is a government policy whose unintended consequence made things worse. The other three are markets producing the wrong amount on their own.
